newsitem.title: USA: IMM currency futures finish mostly lower.
newsitem.headline: IMM currency futures finish mostly lower.

text.p: IMM currency futures finished mostly lower in light trade, as signs that U.S. economic growth was slowing failed to scare traders into selling the dollar off its overnight highs, traders and analysts said.
"We are in a tricky position, because maybe the Federal Reserve won't have to tighten," one currency trader said.
U.S. August durable goods orders were down 3.1 percent, a much sharper drop than traders' average forecast for down 0.1 percent. Weekly jobless claims were higher than expected.
"Maybe jobs creation is starting to slow," he said. "But we do have the continuing pressure on the mark crosses."

Optimism about the European Monetary Union (EMU) continued to weigh on cash marks against the yen, the French franc and the Italian lira, and was considered one of the main reasons for the dollar's support against the European currencies, traders and analysts said.
December mark futures touched off sell-stop orders at the $0.6600 level, or 1.5185 spot marks, and fell to $0.6589 in thin, pit trading.
The contract set a daily low only marginally above a key support level at $0.6587, which is roughly equivalent to the dollar/mark's high of 1.5260/63 spot.

"The 1.2600 (Swiss franc) and 1.5260 (mark) areas are the dollar's high-water marks from mid-July," Michael Malpeded, a currency analyst with Refco, Inc, said. "Above those levels, you would really force corporates to come in to hedge."
A rise to 1.2600 spot Swiss francs could push December Swiss francs near their three-month low around the $0.8005 level. December fell to $0.8030, or roughly 1.2534 spot.
Malpede said the dollar's resiliency during U.S. hours may have already attracted corporates to the forex market.
"You are getting attention, but the fact that there is no follow-through is leading to some questioning," he said.

However, few traders or analysts would dispute that the dollar is poised to continue its rally and that most currency futures are headed lower. The Swiss National Bank's (SNB) decision to lower the Swiss discount rate to 1.0 percent, from 1.50 percent, indicated that the bank was taking a more aggressive stance in easing monetary policy.
Since the beginning of August, the SNB said, it had been supplying the money market with additional liquidity "in order to prevent monetary strain."
In addition, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin repeated his support for a strong U.S. dollar.
Sterling futures held slim losses, stabilizing after Britain reported its best current account surplus in nine years.
Canadian dollar futures were lower on speculation that the Bank of Canada would ease interest rates. Several dealers were aggressive sellers at the $0.7335 level after the opening.

At the end of pit trade, Dec yen was off $0.000015 to $0.009139, marks off $0.0032 to $0.6599, Swiss francs down $0.0077 to $0.8051, sterling off $0.0002 to $1.5600, Canadian dollar down $0.0006 to $0.7337, Aussie dollar up $0.0021 to $0.7909, Mexican peso up $0.000250 to $0.126500.
